title: The protected passed pawn
summary: A passed pawn defended by another pawn ties down the enemy king, and your own king is free to eat the rest.
part.tied.title: The tied-down king
part.tied.summary: The enemy king cannot take the protected pawn and cannot leave its square. Your king goes alone and eats the rest.
part.convert.title: Come back and win
part.convert.summary: After the capture the king returns, and one step of the protected pawn opens the way to the last enemy pawn.
part.base.title: Attacking the base
part.base.summary: When the enemy king goes after the back pawn, the front pawn runs and queens.
part.limits.title: When it does not win
part.limits.summary: Near the corner there is stalemate, and with nothing to eat the free king has no job. Here you defend.
part.finish.title: Summary
part.finish.summary: Three rules for your games, then the whole ending against the machine.
step.t_tied: White to move. Each side has a king and two pawns, but the c5 pawn is passed and defended by the b4 pawn. What is White's plan, and why can Black not do the same?
step.t_tied.hint1: Can the black king take the c5 pawn? Can it walk away from it?
step.t_tied.hint2: Nobody defends the h5 pawn. Count the white king's path to it.
step.square: This is the protected passed pawn. The black king cannot take c5, because b4 defends it. And it cannot walk away: if it leaves the square of c5, from c5 to f8, the pawn runs and queens. The black king is tied to that pawn. My king is tied to nothing.
step.free: So my king goes to eat the h5 pawn: Kf4, Kg3, Kh4 and done. To defend h5 the black king would need g6 or g4, outside the square, and then c6 queens. The protected pawn works on its own without costing a single move, while my king does the job on the other wing.
step.d_tied: Watch the white king fetch the h-pawn while the black king cannot follow.
step.d_tied.m1: Kf4. The king heads for the kingside, where the target is.
step.d_tied.m2: Kf6, to hold g5. If Black goes to g6, he leaves the square and c6 runs.
step.d_tied.m3: Kg3. The road through g4 is closed by the h5 pawn, so I go around through h4.
step.d_tied.m4: Black gives up h5 and goes back near the c-pawn.
step.d_tied.m6: Kd5. The black king can only watch.
step.d_tied.m7: Kxh5. A pawn up, and the protected pawn still holds the black king. Now come back and finish.
step.tiedMove: Your turn. White to move and win. Take the king to the h5 pawn by the shortest road.
step.tiedMove.hint: The white king has work on the kingside. Leave the c5 pawn alone: it already does its job standing still.
step.tiedMove.done: Right. The black king stayed tied to the c5 pawn, and your king ate h5 undisturbed.
step.t_convert: White to move. The h-pawn is already gone. The black king blocks the c-pawn on c6 and defends b5. How does White win the b5 pawn?
step.t_convert.hint1: The white king must reach a square next to b5. By which road?
step.t_convert.hint2: If the c-pawn advances at the right moment, the c5 square becomes free for the white king.
step.convertWhy: The black king on c6 does two things: it stands in front of the c-pawn and defends b5. My king goes to d4 and then d5, beside it. When the black king steps back, I push c6: the pawn is still protected, now by my king, and c5 is free. From c5 my king takes b5.
step.d_convert: Watch the technique: king forward, pawn at the right moment, and the last black pawn falls.
step.d_convert.m1: Kd4. The king comes to the centre, close to the pawns.
step.d_convert.m3: Kd5. The white king arrives next to the c-pawn.
step.d_convert.m5: c6. The pawn advances with the king's support, and c5 is free for me.
step.d_convert.m6: Kc8. The black king cannot touch c6, defended by my king.
step.d_convert.m7: Kc5. Now b5 is attacked and nobody defends it.
step.d_convert.m9: Kxb5. Two pawns against none. The black king cannot hold both.
step.convertMove: Your turn. White to move and win. Bring the king close, push the c-pawn at the right moment and go get b5.
step.convertMove.hint: King first. The c-pawn moves only when the white king stands beside it.
step.convertMove.done: Well done. After c6 the c5 square was free, and your king reached the b5 pawn.
step.t_base: White to move. The black king has reached b4 and attacks the a4 pawn, the base of the protected pawn. Should White worry?
step.t_base.hint1: Look at the square of the b5 pawn. Where is the black king?
step.baseWhy: The black king went after the base and left the square of the front pawn. After b6 the pawn needs two moves to queen, and the black king on b4 cannot reach b8 in time. Attacking the base of a protected pawn almost always costs the square.
step.d_base.m1: b6. The pawn goes on its own; a4 no longer matters.
step.d_base.m4: Kc6. Too late: the king arrives beside the pawn, not in front of it.
step.d_base.m5: b8, queen. The queen is out of the king's reach.
step.baseMove: Your turn, the same idea in the centre. The black king on d4 attacks the c4 pawn. White to move and win.
step.baseMove.hint: The black king has left the square of one of your pawns. Which one?
step.baseMove.done: Right. While the black king stared at c4, the d-pawn queened.
step.t_corner: White to move. The b6 pawn is passed and protected, and the white king is close. Can White still win? Look for the danger before looking for the move.
step.t_corner.hint1: The black king has few squares: a8, b8, c8. Count how many remain when the white king comes close.
step.t_corner.hint2: If the black king has no move and is not in check, what happens?
step.corner: Here the protected pawn does not win. The black king walks between a8 and b8, and every approach by my king takes away its last square. For example: Kd6 Kb8, Kc6 Ka8, and Kc7 is stalemate. If I try b7+, Kb8, and Kb6 is stalemate too. With the pawn on the sixth, next to the rook pawn and the corner, the tablebase gives a draw whatever White plays.
step.cornerMove: Now you defend with Black. The b6 pawn wants to queen and the white king is coming. Black to move and draw.
step.cornerMove.hint: Stay in front of the pawn, close to the corner. Moving the king away lets b7 run.
step.cornerMove.done: Right. In front of the pawn and near the corner the black king is safe: the white king cannot come in without stalemating.
step.noTarget: Another position that does not win. The b4 pawn is passed and protected by c3, but look at the black pawn on c4: it covers b3 and d3, and the black king defends it from d5. My king has nothing to eat, and the black king cannot take b4. The protected passer only wins when the free king has a target. Here there is none: a draw.
step.targetMove: You play Black again. Black to move and draw. Keep the white king away from c4.
step.targetMove.hint: The black king must stay near c4 and the d4 square, where the white king wants to come in. Do not drift towards the b-file.
step.targetMove.done: Correct. Kc6? would let the white king come closer with Ke3, and Black could no longer close the road to d4. Near c4 and d4, the draw holds.
step.recap: To sum up: the c5 pawn is protected and ties down the black king. So my king is free to go to the kingside and eat h5, and then come back to finish on the queenside.
step.rules: Three rules. First: the protected passed pawn needs no help; it keeps the enemy king inside its square. Second: your king is the free piece; use it to eat the pawns on the other wing, and only then come back. Third: it does not win by itself near the corner, because of stalemate, nor when your king has nothing to attack.
step.recapMove: White to move and win. Start by sending the king the right way.
step.recapMove.hint: The target is on h5. The c5 pawn stays where it is.
step.recapMove.done: Right. The king heads for h5, and the black king cannot follow without letting the c-pawn go.
step.finish: Now play the whole ending against the machine. Eat the h-pawn, come back, and win the b5 pawn.
ex.e01: White to move and win. The black king attacks the base of the protected pawn. What is the clearest answer?
ex.e01.hint: The black king is outside the square of the b5 pawn.
ex.e01.solution: b6! The black king left the square to attack a4, and the pawn queens before it can get back: b6, b7, b8. King moves also win, but the push settles it at once.
ex.e02: Black to move and draw. The b6 pawn is protected and the white king is coming. Where should the black king stand?
ex.e02.hint: Near the corner and in front of the pawn.
ex.e02.solution: Kb7, in front of the pawn (Kd6 and Kd7 also hold). Kb5? or Kc5? lose: the king leaves b8 behind and b7 queens. In the corner, the white king cannot come in without stalemating.
ex.e03: White to move and win. The g5 pawn is alone. Go and get it before the black king arrives.
ex.e03.hint: The black king wants to reach f6 to defend g5, and f6 is inside the square of the c5 pawn. Be faster.
ex.e03.solution: Kg4! attacks g5 at once, and next comes Kxg5. Kg3? is slow: with Ke6 and Kf6 the black king defends g5 without leaving the square of c5, and the tablebase says draw.
ex.e04: White to move and win. The h-pawn is already gone. How does White win the b5 pawn?
ex.e04.hint: King first, next to the c-pawn. Then the pawn advances and frees a square for the king.
ex.e04.solution: Kd4, Kd5 and, when the black king leaves c6, c6! The pawn is protected by the king, c5 is free, and the white king goes to c5 to eat b5.
ex.e05: Black to move and win. Now Black has the protected passed pawn: c4, defended by b5. What is the plan?
ex.e05.hint: The c4 pawn ties down the white king. The black king is free. Where is the target?
ex.e05.solution: Kf5 and Kg4: the black king goes to eat the h4 pawn. The white king cannot defend it, because it must stay in the square of the c4 pawn. The same idea as in the first part, with colours reversed.
ex.e06: White to move and win. The black king attacks g4, the base of the f5 pawn.
ex.e06.hint: Look at the square of the f5 pawn.
ex.e06.solution: f6! If Kxg4, f7 and f8 queens: the black king is too far away. Attacking the base cost him the square.
ex.e07: White to move and win. The white king is already on d5, next to the c-pawn. Which move opens the road to b5?
ex.e07.hint: The white king needs the c5 square, and the pawn itself is standing on it.
ex.e07.solution: c6! The pawn advances with the king's support, frees c5, and then Kc5 and Kxb5. The black king cannot take c6 while the white king defends it.
ex.e08: White to move and win. The a6 pawn is passed and protected, but Black has two passed pawns, on e4 and h5. Only one move wins.
ex.e08.hint: The black king is tied to the a6 pawn. The white king must stop both black pawns.
ex.e08.solution: Kg3! The king stays close to both pawns: it catches h5 and does not let e4 through. a7? is hasty: the black king takes the pawn and the tablebase says draw. After Kg3, Kf4 goes after the e-pawn.
ex.e09: White to move and win. The white king is far from the h5 pawn. Which way should it go?
ex.e09.hint: The h5 pawn is passed too. The white king has two jobs: stop that pawn and eat it.
ex.e09.solution: Ke2 (Ke1 and Kd2 also win), and the king heads for f3, g3 and h4. Kc2? loses: the h-pawn runs with h4 and the white king no longer catches it. The c5 pawn takes care of the black king; the white king takes care of the rest.
ex.e10: Black to move and draw. White has a protected passed pawn on a4, but it is a rook pawn and the white king is far away. Only one move holds. The position comes from an old study that IsaacWiebeSupreme's Lichess study calls "Dedrele Study".
ex.e10.hint: The black king must stay near the a-pawn and, at the same time, be ready to face the white king as it approaches.
ex.e10.solution: Kd6! and, after Kf3, Kd5! With Kc6? White plays Kg3! and arrives in time. After Kd6, if a5, the black king goes to c5 and b6 and eats the a-pawn. The protected rook pawn is the case where the defender is saved most often.
key.tied: The tied-down king: White wins with either side to move. A reduced version of the Reuben Fine and Pal Benko diagram shown on Wikipedia (without the a-pawns).
key.convert: After the capture: king beside the pawn, c6 at the right moment, and the king reaches b5.
key.base: The black king attacks the base and leaves the square: b6 queens.
key.corner: Pawn on the sixth, next to the corner: a draw by stalemate. As in IsaacWiebeSupreme's study.
key.noTarget: The black c4 pawn stays defended and the white king has no target: a draw.
key.dedrle: The "Dedrele Study", as it appears in IsaacWiebeSupreme's study: Black to move, and only Kd6 draws.
history: The protected passed pawn is in every endgame book: Dvoretsky gives it a section in the pawn endgame chapter of his manual, and Jesús de la Villa puts it among the hundred endgames every player must know. Wikipedia shows a position from Reuben Fine and Pal Benko's book in which White wins with either side to move: the black king cannot be on both wings at once, defending its own passed pawn and stopping the protected one. The version in this lesson, with fewer pawns, was checked against the tablebase. The case of the protected rook pawn, which sometimes does not win, appears in an old study that Lichess records as "Dedrele Study", and it is among the exercises.
practice: Now the real ending: the protected c5 pawn, the lonely black g5 pawn, and your king still on e2. Tie the black king down with the pawn, eat the g-pawn and come back. Pick your pace and go.
